claim: GluA4-knockout mice had ~80% reduced mossy fiber to granule cell synaptic transmission.
source: Notably, GluA4-knockout mice had ~80% reduced mossy fiber to granule cell synaptic transmission.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data showing EPSC amplitude reduction in Figure 1B-C, with quantification showing 13.4 ± 1.1 pA vs. 76.2 ± 7.5 pA (p < 0.0001).

claim: The fidelity of granule cell spike output was markedly decreased in GluA4-knockout mice despite attenuated tonic inhibition and increased NMDA receptor-mediated transmission.
source: The fidelity of granule cell spike output was markedly decreased despite attenuated tonic inhibition and increased NMDA receptor-mediated transmission.
evidence: The manuscript presents data on GC spike output (Figure 4), tonic inhibition (Figure 2), and NMDAR transmission (Figure 5) showing these compensatory changes.

claim: Deletion of GluA4 impairs granule cell expansion coding according to computational network modeling.
source: Computational network modeling incorporating these changes revealed that deletion of GluA4 impairs granule cell expansion coding, which is important for pattern separation and associative learning.
evidence: The manuscript presents computational modeling results in Figure 6 showing reduced expansion coding in the KO model.

claim: GluA4-knockout mice failed to form associative memories during delay eyeblink conditioning.
source: On a behavioral level, while locomotor coordination was generally spared, GluA4-knockout mice failed to form associative memories during delay eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data in Figure 8 showing absence of conditioned responses in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: Locomotor coordination was generally spared in GluA4-knockout mice.
source: On a behavioral level, while locomotor coordination was generally spared, GluA4-knockout mice failed to form associative memories during delay eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7 showing largely intact locomotor behavior in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: GluA4 is the major AMPAR subunit at MF→GC synapses.
source: Within the cerebellar cortex, this AMPAR subunit has been described in Bergmann glia (Saab et al., 2012) and in GCs (Mosbacher et al., 1994), where GluA4 is the major AMPAR subunit at MF→GC synapses (Delvendahl et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Delvendahl et al., 2019).

claim: GluA4 confers rapid kinetics and large conductance to AMPARs.
source: The GluA4 subunit confers rapid kinetics and large conductance to AMPARs (Mosbacher et al., 1994; Swanson et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Mosbacher et al., 1994; Swanson et al., 1997).

claim: GluA4 expression is confined to few types of neurons in the adult brain.
source: Yet, its expression is confined to few types of neurons in the adult brain (Keinänen et al., 1990; Monyer et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Keinänen et al., 1990; Monyer et al., 1991).

claim: Deletion of GluA4 impairs excitatory input to certain neurons in the auditory brainstem.
source: Deletion of GluA4 impairs excitatory input to certain neurons in the auditory brainstem (Yang et al., 2011), the thalamus (Paz et al., 2011; Seol and Kuner, 2015), and the hippocampus (Fuchs et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Yang et al., 2011).

claim: Deletion of GluA4 impairs excitatory input to certain neurons in the thalamus.
source: Deletion of GluA4 impairs excitatory input to certain neurons in the auditory brainstem (Yang et al., 2011), the thalamus (Paz et al., 2011; Seol and Kuner, 2015), and the hippocampus (Fuchs et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Paz et al., 2011; Seol and Kuner, 2015).

claim: Deletion of GluA4 impairs excitatory input to certain neurons in the hippocampus.
source: Deletion of GluA4 impairs excitatory input to certain neurons in the auditory brainstem (Yang et al., 2011), the thalamus (Paz et al., 2011; Seol and Kuner, 2015), and the hippocampus (Fuchs et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Fuchs et al., 2007).

claim: Granule cells heavily express GluA4 in the cerebellum.
source: In the cerebellum, granule cells (GCs)—the most abundant neurons in the mammalian brain—heavily express GluA4 (Cathala et al., 2005; Hollmann and Heinemann, 1994; Mosbacher et al., 1994; Schwenk et al., 2014), but the significance of GluA4 for GCs and cerebellar circuit function remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cathala et al., 2005; Hollmann and Heinemann, 1994; Mosbacher et al., 1994; Schwenk et al., 2014).

claim: Granule cells are the most abundant neurons in the mammalian brain.
source: In the cerebellum, granule cells (GCs)—the most abundant neurons in the mammalian brain—heavily express GluA4 (Cathala et al., 2005; Hollmann and Heinemann, 1994; Mosbacher et al., 1994; Schwenk et al., 2014), but the significance of GluA4 for GCs and cerebellar circuit function remains unclear.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience.

claim: The cerebellum plays an important role in sensorimotor integration, motor coordination, motor learning and timing, as well as cognition.
source: The cerebellum plays an important role in sensorimotor integration, motor coordination, motor learning and timing, as well as cognition (Diedrichsen et al., 2019; Raymond and Medina, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Diedrichsen et al., 2019; Raymond and Medina, 2018).

claim: The cerebellar cortex achieves millisecond precision in the calibration and timing of movement.
source: The underlying computations are very fast, allowing millisecond precision in the calibration and timing of movement (Heck et al., 2013; Osborne et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Heck et al., 2013; Osborne et al., 2007).

claim: Mossy fibers contact a large number of granule cells in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Sensory and motor information enter the cerebellar cortex via mossy fibers (MFs) that contact a large number of GCs.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Granule cells greatly outnumber mossy fibers, providing a large expansion of coding space.
source: These small, numerous neurons greatly outnumber MFs, thus providing a large expansion of coding space (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969).

claim: Granule cells relay information via their parallel fibers to Purkinje cells.
source: GCs relay information via their parallel fibers (PFs) to Purkinje cells (PCs), the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex.
source: GCs relay information via their parallel fibers (PFs) to Purkinje cells (PCs), the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: The MF→GC synapse has evolved mechanisms allowing for transmission with exceptionally high rates and precision.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that the MF→GC synapse has evolved mechanisms allowing for transmission with exceptionally high rates and precision (Delvendahl and Hallermann, 2016; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Rancz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Delvendahl and Hallermann, 2016; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Rancz et al., 2007).

claim: GluA4-KO GCs displayed strongly diminished synaptic responses upon MF stimulation.
source: GluA4-KO GCs displayed strongly diminished synaptic responses upon MF stimulation, with an ~80% reduction in excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs; 13.4 ± 1.1 pA vs. 76.2 ± 7.5 pA; p < 0.0001; Figure 1B–C; Delvendahl et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1B-C showing this reduction.

claim: The EPSC decay was slower in GluA4-KO GCs than in WT.
source: Consistent with the fast kinetics of GluA4-containing AMPARs (Mosbacher et al., 1994), the EPSC decay was slower in GluA4-KO GCs than in WT (3.1 ± 0.3 ms vs. 1.8 ± 0.2 ms; p < 0.001; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1C showing this difference in decay kinetics.

claim: At MF→GoC connections, EPSC amplitudes and decay kinetics were comparable between WT and GluA4-KO.
source: At MF→GoC connections (Figure 1D), EPSC amplitudes and decay kinetics were comparable between WT and GluA4-KO (Figure 1E–F), suggesting that GluA4 does not contribute to MF→GoC transmission.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1E-F showing no significant differences.

claim: GluA4 does not contribute to MF→GoC transmission.
source: At MF→GoC connections (Figure 1D), EPSC amplitudes and decay kinetics were comparable between WT and GluA4-KO (Figure 1E–F), suggesting that GluA4 does not contribute to MF→GoC transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference in EPSC properties between WT and KO at MF→GoC synapses.

claim: PF inputs to GoCs were similar between WT and GluA4-KO mice.
source: We therefore investigated PF inputs to GoCs (PF→GoC synapses; Figure 1G), which were similar between WT and GluA4-KO mice (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1H-I showing no significant differences.

claim: Spontaneous EPSCs and paired-pulse ratios were not altered in GoCs of GluA4-KO mice.
source: Consistent with the similar EPSC amplitudes, spontaneous EPSCs and paired-pulse ratios were also not altered in GoCs of GluA4-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing no significant differences.

claim: Purkinje cells do not express GluA4.
source: Whereas PCs do not express GluA4 (Lambolez et al., 1992), loss of this AMPAR subunit in Bergmann glial cells might impact PF→PC transmission (Saab et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Lambolez et al., 1992).

claim: The slope of the stimulus-response relationship at PF→PC synapses was comparable between WT and GluA4-KO genotypes.
source: The slope of the stimulus-response relationship was comparable between genotypes (Figure 1L; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which indicates normal recruitment of PFs.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1L showing no significant difference.

claim: EPSC decay kinetics at PF→PC synapses were similar between WT and KO PCs.
source: Likewise, EPSC decay kinetics (Figure 1L) as well as spontaneous EPSC amplitudes and paired-pulse ratios were similar between WT and KO PCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that GluA4 does not contribute directly to PF→PC synaptic transmission.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing no significant differences.

claim: GluA4 does not contribute directly to PF→PC synaptic transmission.
source: Likewise, EPSC decay kinetics (Figure 1L) as well as spontaneous EPSC amplitudes and paired-pulse ratios were similar between WT and KO PCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that GluA4 does not contribute directly to PF→PC synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of differences in PF→PC synaptic properties between WT and KO.

claim: PF output is functionally intact in GluA4-KO mice.
source: The recordings from PF→GoC and PF→PC synapses thus indicate that PF output is functionally intact in GluA4-KO mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal properties of PF→GoC and PF→PC synapses in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: Gross cerebellar organization was unaltered in GluA4-KO mice.
source: Moreover, gross cerebellar organization was unaltered in GluA4-KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript presents anatomical data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing no obvious differences.

claim: GluA4 is indispensable for fast neurotransmission at MF→GC synapses.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that GluA4 is indispensable for fast neurotransmission at MF→GC synapses and suggest a GC-specific impairment of excitatory transmission at the cerebellar input layer in GluA4-KO mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the strong reduction in MF→GC transmission and slower kinetics in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: Under control conditions, GluA4-KO GCs showed higher firing frequencies than WT, reflecting increased excitability.
source: Under control conditions, GluA4-KO GCs showed higher firing frequencies than WT, reflecting increased excitability (linear mixed effects analysis: current × genotype interaction, χ2(1) = 35.48, p < 0.001; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2B-C showing increased firing in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: The input-output relationship was similar between KO and WT GCs in the presence of bicuculline.
source: Interestingly, the input-output relationship was similar between KO and WT GCs in the presence of bicuculline (linear mixed effects analysis: current × genotype interaction, χ2(1) = 0.61, p = 0.43; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2B-C showing no significant difference in the presence of bicuculline.

claim: Blocking inhibition increased the gain and reduced the rheobase current in WT GCs.
source: Blocking inhibition increased the gain and reduced the rheobase current in WT (Figure 2D), consistent with previous studies (Hamann et al., 2002; Rothman et al., 2009; Rudolph et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2D and cites previous studies (Hamann et al., 2002; Rothman et al., 2009; Rudolph et al., 2020).

claim: Bicuculline had little effect on gain and rheobase in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: By contrast, bicuculline had little effect on gain and rheobase in GluA4-KO GCs (ANOVA gain: genotype × drug: F = 4.24, p = 0.041, η2p = 0.028; rheobase: genotype × drug: F = 2.00, p = 0.16, η2p = 0.014; Figure 2D), indicating that tonic inhibition is reduced in these mice.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2D showing minimal effect of bicuculline in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: Tonic inhibition is reduced in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: By contrast, bicuculline had little effect on gain and rheobase in GluA4-KO GCs (ANOVA gain: genotype × drug: F = 4.24, p = 0.041, η2p = 0.028; rheobase: genotype × drug: F = 2.00, p = 0.16, η2p = 0.014; Figure 2D), indicating that tonic inhibition is reduced in these mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of bicuculline on GluA4-KO GC excitability.

claim: Tonic GABAAR activation leads to shunting inhibition of GCs that controls their responses to excitatory input.
source: Tonic GABAAR activation leads to shunting inhibition of GCs that may affect their responses to excitatory input (Brickley et al., 2001; Mitchell and Silver, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Brickley et al., 2001; Mitchell and Silver, 2003).

claim: GluA4-KO GCs had a smaller root-mean-square noise of the baseline holding current compared with WT.
source: Indeed, GluA4-KO GCs had a smaller root-mean-square noise of the baseline holding current and smaller bicuculline-sensitive conductance compared with WT (39.0 ± 9.6 pS/pF vs. 83.0 ± 13.3 pS/pF, p = 0.022; Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2E-F showing reduced tonic inhibitory conductance.

claim: GluA4-KO GCs had smaller bicuculline-sensitive conductance compared with WT.
source: Indeed, GluA4-KO GCs had a smaller root-mean-square noise of the baseline holding current and smaller bicuculline-sensitive conductance compared with WT (39.0 ± 9.6 pS/pF vs. 83.0 ± 13.3 pS/pF, p = 0.022; Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2E-F showing reduced tonic inhibitory conductance.

claim: Tonic GABAAR-mediated inhibition is reduced in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: These findings show that tonic GABAAR-mediated inhibition is reduced in GluA4-KO GCs, in line with the lack of effect of bicuculline on the input-output relationship in these animals.
evidence: This is concluded from the reduced bicuculline-sensitive conductance in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: The GABAAR α6-subunit mediates tonic inhibition of GCs.
source: The GABAAR α6-subunit mediates tonic inhibition of GCs (Brickley et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Brickley et al., 2001).

claim: Western blot analyses revealed slightly lower α6 GABAAR levels in GluA4-KO cerebella.
source: Interestingly, Western blot analyses revealed slightly lower α6 GABAAR levels in GluA4-KO cerebella (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with the reduction of tonic inhibition in GCs.
evidence: The manuscript presents Western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing reduced α6 GABAAR expression.

claim: The amplitudes and frequencies of spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents were not different between WT and GluA4-KO GCs.
source: By contrast, the amplitudes and frequencies of spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) were not different between WT and GluA4-KO GCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that phasic inhibition is not altered.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing no significant differences.

claim: Phasic inhibition is not altered in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: By contrast, the amplitudes and frequencies of spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) were not different between WT and GluA4-KO GCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that phasic inhibition is not altered.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference in sIPSC properties between WT and KO GCs.

claim: The strongly impaired excitatory synaptic input to GluA4-KO GCs is accompanied by a modulation of tonic inhibition, resulting in an increased input-output relationship.
source: Thus, the strongly impaired excitatory synaptic input to GluA4-KO GCs is accompanied by a modulation of tonic inhibition, resulting in an increased input-output relationship.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of reduced excitatory input, reduced tonic inhibition, and increased excitability in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: EPSC amplitudes were strongly diminished in GluA4-KO GCs, as were EPSP amplitudes.
source: As expected, EPSC amplitudes were strongly diminished in GluA4-KO GCs, as were EPSP amplitudes (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 3B-C showing reduced EPSC and EPSP amplitudes.

claim: The amplitude reduction relative to WT was smaller for EPSPs than for EPSCs in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: Intriguingly, the amplitude reduction relative to WT was smaller for EPSPs than for EPSCs (69.4 ± 2.1% vs. 80.6 ± 1%, p < 0.001, d = −1.02; Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 3C showing this differential reduction.

claim: Bicuculline increased EPSP amplitudes in WT, but not in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: To test if reduced tonic inhibition underlies this effect, we recorded EPSPs in the presence of bicuculline, which increased EPSP amplitudes in WT, but not in GluA4-KO GCs (ANOVA drug × genotype: F = 8.00, p = 0.005, η2p = 0.056; Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 3D-E showing differential effect of bicuculline.

claim: Bicuculline enhanced EPSP amplitudes during high-frequency train stimulation in WT, but not in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: We also observed that bicuculline enhanced EPSP amplitudes during high-frequency train stimulation in WT, but not in GluA4-KO GCs (ANOVA drug × genotype: F = 48.77, p < 0.001, η2p = 0.19; Figure 3F–G).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 3F-G showing differential effect of bicuculline during trains.

claim: Shunting inhibition reduces postsynaptic depolarization in response to excitatory input in WT, but not in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: These results demonstrate that shunting inhibition reduces postsynaptic depolarization in response to excitatory input in WT, but not in GluA4-KO GCs.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of bicuculline on EPSPs in WT vs. GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: The reduced tonic inhibition upon loss of the major AMPAR subunit at MF→GC synapses augments synaptic depolarization in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: We conclude that the reduced tonic inhibition upon loss of the major AMPAR subunit at MF→GC synapses augments synaptic depolarization in GluA4-KO GCs.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of reduced tonic inhibition and differential EPSP amplitudes in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: WT GCs showed increasing firing frequencies upon 100–300 Hz stimulation.
source: WT GCs showed increasing firing frequencies upon 100–300 Hz stimulation (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 4B-C showing frequency-dependent firing.

claim: MF stimulation-evoked spikes in GluA4-KO GCs occurred at reduced frequency compared to WT.
source: We also observed MF stimulation-evoked spikes in GluA4-KO GCs, albeit at reduced frequency (ANOVA genotype: F = 23.48; p < 0.0001, η2p = 0.15; Figure 4C) and in fewer cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 4C showing reduced firing frequency in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: MF stimulation-evoked spikes in GluA4-KO GCs occurred in fewer cells compared to WT.
source: We also observed MF stimulation-evoked spikes in GluA4-KO GCs, albeit at reduced frequency (ANOVA genotype: F = 23.48; p < 0.0001, η2p = 0.15; Figure 4C) and in fewer cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 4D showing fewer spiking cells in GluA4-KO.

claim: GC spikes elicited by high-frequency MF→GC stimulation occurred with a longer delay in GluA4-KO compared to WT.
source: The GC spikes elicited by high-frequency MF→GC stimulation were not only reduced in number, but also occurred with a longer delay compared to WT (ANOVA genotype: F = 26.26; p < 0.0001, η2p = 0.29; Figure 4E-F).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 4E-F showing increased spike delay in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: GluA4-KO GCs need to summate more EPSPs to reach spike threshold.
source: GluA4-KO GCs hence need to summate more EPSPs to reach spike threshold (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), leading to reduced reliability and impaired temporal precision of GC spikes.
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing increased EPSP summation requirement.

claim: GluA4-containing AMPARs control the timing and reliability of EPSP-spike coupling at the cerebellar input layer.
source: Together, these data show a strong reduction of spiking frequency and temporal precision in GluA4-KO GCs upon high-frequency synaptic input, and establish that GluA4-containing AMPARs control the timing and reliability of EPSP-spike coupling at the cerebellar input layer.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of reduced spike frequency, increased delay, and reduced reliability in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: Isolated NMDAR-mediated MF→GC EPSCs were larger in GluA4-KO than in WT GCs.
source: Indeed, isolated NMDAR-mediated MF→GC EPSCs were larger in GluA4-KO than in WT GCs (37.2 ± 2.1 pA vs. 27.5 ± 2.1 pA; p = 0.0026; d = 1.04; Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 5A-B showing increased NMDAR-EPSCs in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: Statistical moments analysis of quanta indicated an increase in presynaptic release sites without apparent changes in release probability or quantal size in GluA4-KO.
source: Whereas NMDAR-EPSC paired-pulse ratios were similar between GluA4-KO and WT MF→GC synapses, statistical moments analysis of quanta (Holler et al., 2021) indicated an increase in presynaptic release sites without apparent changes in release probability or quantal size in GluA4-KO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing increased release sites.

claim: AMPAR-EPSCs were strongly decreased in GluA4-KO GCs during 100 Hz train stimulation.
source: As expected, AMPAR-EPSCs were strongly decreased in GluA4-KO GCs (Figure 5C), leading to a pronounced reduction of cumulative EPSC charge during the train (0.9 ± 0.1 pC vs. 3.4 ± 0.2 pC; p < 0.0001; d = −3.05; Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 5C-D showing reduced AMPAR-mediated charge transfer.

claim: NMDAR-EPSCs and cumulative EPSC charge were increased in GluA4-KO GCs during 100 Hz train stimulation.
source: By contrast, NMDAR-EPSCs and cumulative EPSC charge were increased in GluA4-KO GCs (8.7 ± 0.9 pC vs. 5.6 ± 0.4 pC; p = 0.0063; d = 0.92; Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data in Figure 5D showing increased NMDAR-mediated charge transfer.

claim: The model with GluA4-KO GAMPA and GNMDA and reduced tonic conductance displayed lower firing frequencies over the entire range of MF inputs compared to WT.
source: The model with GluA4-KO GAMPA and GNMDA and reduced tonic conductance displayed lower firing frequencies over the entire range of MF inputs (Figure 5G; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 5G showing reduced firing in the KO model.

claim: The KO model had an ~44% reduced maximum firing frequency compared with WT.
source: Compared with WT, the KO model had an ~44% reduced maximum firing frequency (186.1 Hz vs. 336.4 Hz) and an ~17 Hz increased offset, similar to the experimental findings (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results showing reduced maximum firing frequency in the KO model.

claim: Spikes occurred with a longer delay in the KO GC model across all simulated MF frequencies.
source: As in the current-clamp recordings (Figure 4F), spikes occurred with a longer delay in the KO GC model across all simulated MF frequencies (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing increased spike delay in the KO model.

claim: Reduced tonic inhibition and enhanced GNMDA each contribute ~20% to the maximum spiking frequency of the KO model.
source: In both scenarios, firing frequencies were reduced in relation to the KO model, with each mechanism contributing ~20% to the maximum spiking frequency of the KO model (Figure 5H–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 5H-I showing individual contributions of inhibition and NMDAR changes.

claim: The strongly reduced GAMPA of the KO model compromises the synchrony of MF and GC spikes.
source: Analysis of presynaptic and postsynaptic spike trains revealed that the strongly reduced GAMPA of the KO model compromises the synchrony of MF and GC spikes (approximately twofold reduction in spike synchronization Mulansky et al., 2015; Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and that the reduced tonic inhibition and GNMDA enhancement in GluA4-KO facilitate MF→GC synaptic information transfer at low input frequencies, albeit at a reduced level (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing reduced spike synchronization.

claim: Reduced tonic inhibition and GNMDA enhancement in GluA4-KO facilitate MF→GC synaptic information transfer at low input frequencies, albeit at a reduced level.
source: Analysis of presynaptic and postsynaptic spike trains revealed that the strongly reduced GAMPA of the KO model compromises the synchrony of MF and GC spikes (approximately twofold reduction in spike synchronization Mulansky et al., 2015; Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and that the reduced tonic inhibition and GNMDA enhancement in GluA4-KO facilitate MF→GC synaptic information transfer at low input frequencies, albeit at a reduced level (Figure 5G–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 5G-H showing facilitation at low frequencies.

claim: Synaptic and non-synaptic mechanisms cooperatively counteract the impaired spiking output of GluA4-KO GCs, but are insufficient to compensate for the pronounced impairment of synaptic excitation.
source: Thus, although MF→GC AMPAR-EPSCs are strongly reduced, synaptic and non-synaptic mechanisms cooperatively counteract the impaired spiking output of GluA4-KO GCs. However, both mechanisms are insufficient to compensate for the pronounced impairment of synaptic excitation caused by the deletion of GluA4.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental and modeling results showing partial compensation but persistent deficits.

claim: GCs receive sparse input from only on average four MFs.
source: GCs receive sparse input from only on average four MFs, and vastly outnumber afferent MFs, with an expansion ratio of ~200:1 (Herculano-Houzel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Herculano-Houzel, 2009).

claim: GCs vastly outnumber afferent MFs, with an expansion ratio of ~200:1.
source: GCs receive sparse input from only on average four MFs, and vastly outnumber afferent MFs, with an expansion ratio of ~200:1 (Herculano-Houzel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Herculano-Houzel, 2009).

claim: The abundance of GCs and their sparse connectivity make the GC layer ideally suited for sparsening and expanding of MF inputs, leading to a higher-dimensional representation of information.
source: The abundance of GCs and their sparse connectivity make the GC layer ideally suited for sparsening and expanding of MF inputs, leading to a higher-dimensional representation of information (Albus, 1971; Lanore et al., 2021; Marr, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work (Albus, 1971; Lanore et al., 2021; Marr, 1969).

claim: The transformation of neural coding at the GC layer is thought to enable effective pattern separation and facilitate associative learning in downstream circuits.
source: This transformation of neural coding is thought to enable effective pattern separation and facilitate associative learning in downstream circuits (Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019).

claim: Effective excitation of GCs ensures a high encoding capacity and lossless information transfer at the GC layer.
source: Because effective excitation of GCs ensures a high encoding capacity and lossless information transfer at the GC layer (Billings et al., 2014), deletion of GluA4 may compromise pattern separation and learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Billings et al., 2014).

claim: Both control and KO models showed a similar increase in spatial sparseness of GC activity patterns compared with MF activity patterns.
source: Both control and KO models showed a similar increase in spatial sparseness of GC activity patterns compared with MF activity patterns (Figure 6C), indicating that deletion of GluA4 did not affect population sparsening.
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 6C showing similar sparseness in both models.

claim: Deletion of GluA4 did not affect population sparsening in the feedforward network model.
source: Both control and KO models showed a similar increase in spatial sparseness of GC activity patterns compared with MF activity patterns (Figure 6C), indicating that deletion of GluA4 did not affect population sparsening.
evidence: This is concluded from the similar sparseness values in control and KO models.

claim: The normalized total variance—reflecting the expansion of coding space—was strongly reduced in the GluA4-KO model.
source: The normalized total variance—reflecting the expansion of coding space—was strongly reduced in the GluA4-KO model (Figure 6D), suggesting that the increased spiking threshold of GluA4-KO GCs leads to a strong reduction of coding space at the cerebellar input layer.
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 6D showing reduced total variance in the KO model.

claim: The increased spiking threshold of GluA4-KO GCs leads to a strong reduction of coding space at the cerebellar input layer.
source: The normalized total variance—reflecting the expansion of coding space—was strongly reduced in the GluA4-KO model (Figure 6D), suggesting that the increased spiking threshold of GluA4-KO GCs leads to a strong reduction of coding space at the cerebellar input layer.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced total variance in the KO model.

claim: Learning speed was reduced over the full range of model parameters when using the GluA4-KO synaptic conductances.
source: Learning speed was reduced over the full range of model parameters when using the GluA4-KO synaptic conductances (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 6G showing reduced learning speed in the KO model.

claim: GC activity accelerated learning only at high correlation levels and active fraction of MFs in the GluA4-KO model.
source: Notably, GC activity accelerated learning only at high correlation levels and active fraction of MFs (white borders in Figure 6G), in contrast to the previously published model (Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript presents modeling results in Figure 6G showing limited conditions for learning acceleration in the KO model.

claim: The total variance, but not population sparseness, closely predicted learning speed in the feedforward network model.
source: Moreover, the total variance (Figure 6D), but not population sparseness, closely predicted learning speed, suggesting that the strong decrease of MF→GC transmission impairs learning speed by reducing the coding space.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between total variance and learning speed in the modeling results.

claim: The strong decrease of MF→GC transmission impairs learning speed by reducing the coding space.
source: Moreover, the total variance (Figure 6D), but not population sparseness, closely predicted learning speed, suggesting that the strong decrease of MF→GC transmission impairs learning speed by reducing the coding space.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing correlation between total variance and learning speed.

claim: GluA4 facilitates expansion coding in a feedforward MF-GC network model without major effects on population sparseness.
source: Together, our data indicate that GluA4 facilitates expansion coding in a feedforward MF-GC network model without major effects on population sparseness.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results showing reduced total variance but similar sparseness in the KO model.

claim: The effects of GluA4 deletion on GC population coding may improve pattern separation and thus speed learning.
source: These effects on GC population coding may improve pattern separation and thus speed learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing reduced learning speed in the KO model.

claim: GluA4-KO mice walked similarly to size-matched WT littermates without obvious gait ataxia.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that GluA4-KO mice walked similarly to size-matched WT littermates without obvious gait ataxia (Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral observations and video evidence (Video 1).

claim: GluA4-KO mice tended to walk more slowly than controls.
source: GluA4-KO mice tended to walk more slowly than controls, but across walking speeds, stride lengths were comparable in mice of both genotypes (Figure 7D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7D-E showing this tendency.

claim: Across walking speeds, stride lengths were comparable in GluA4-KO and WT mice.
source: GluA4-KO mice tended to walk more slowly than controls, but across walking speeds, stride lengths were comparable in mice of both genotypes (Figure 7D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7D-E showing comparable stride lengths.

claim: Paw trajectories measured by continuous forward velocity were intact in GluA4-KO mice.
source: Paw trajectories measured by continuous forward velocity were also intact (Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7F-G showing normal paw trajectories.

claim: Vertical paw motion was largely normal in GluA4-KO mice, although there was a small degree of hyperflexion across walking speeds.
source: Vertical paw motion was also largely normal (Figure 7H–I), although there was a small degree of hyperflexion across walking speeds (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7H-I showing largely normal vertical motion with minor hyperflexion.

claim: No differences in interlimb coordination were observed between WT and GluA4-KO mice during normal walking.
source: We also explored interlimb coordination, which is often disrupted by cerebellar damage (Machado et al., 2020a; Machado et al., 2015; Morton and Bastian, 2007), during normal walking. We did not observe any differences between WT and GluA4-KO mice, with both genotypes displaying a symmetrical trot pattern across walking speeds (Figure 7J–K).
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7J-K showing similar interlimb coordination.

claim: Both WT and GluA4-KO mice displayed a symmetrical trot pattern across walking speeds.
source: We did not observe any differences between WT and GluA4-KO mice, with both genotypes displaying a symmetrical trot pattern across walking speeds (Figure 7J–K).
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7J-K showing symmetrical trot patterns.

claim: Locomotor coordination was largely spared in GluA4-KO mice despite the pronounced impairment of synaptic excitation at the cerebellar input layer.
source: Thus, locomotor coordination was largely spared in GluA4-KO mice despite the pronounced impairment of synaptic excitation at the cerebellar input layer.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of normal locomotion and impaired MF→GC transmission.

claim: The US elicited a similar response in mice of both genotypes during eyeblink conditioning.
source: The US elicited a similar response in mice of both genotypes (p = 0.36; Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data in Figure 8B showing similar unconditioned responses.

claim: WT mice displayed a continuous increase in the percentage of trials with a conditioned response during eyeblink conditioning.
source: WT mice displayed a continuous increase in the percentage of trials with a conditioned response (CR; Figure 8D), demonstrating associative memory formation.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data in Figure 8D showing learning in WT mice.

claim: GluA4-KO mice failed to develop CRs over the 10 training sessions during eyeblink conditioning.
source: Strikingly, GluA4-KO mice failed to develop CRs over the 10 training sessions (Figure 8C and D, top), indicating a lack of associative learning in the eyeblink conditioning task.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data in Figure 8C-D showing absence of learning in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: GluA4-KO mice failed to show any learned eyelid closures in response to the CS in CS-only trials.
source: Analysis of CS-only trials revealed that, in contrast to WT animals, which had developed well-timed CRs by the end of training, GluA4-KO mice failed to show any learned eyelid closures in response to the CS (Figure 8E–F, top).
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data in Figure 8E-F showing absence of CRs in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: CRs were absent in GluA4-KO mice when using whisker stimulation as a CS.
source: To rule out the possibility that impaired vision was contributing to this effect (Gründer et al., 2000; Qin and Pourcho, 1999), we repeated the eyeblink conditioning experiments in a new set of mice using whisker stimulation as a CS. Again, CRs were absent in GluA4-KO mice (Figure 8C–F, bottom), demonstrating that GluA4 is required for eyeblink conditioning independent of CS modality.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data in Figure 8C-F showing absence of learning with whisker CS.

claim: GluA4 is required for eyeblink conditioning independent of CS modality.
source: Again, CRs were absent in GluA4-KO mice (Figure 8C–F, bottom), demonstrating that GluA4 is required for eyeblink conditioning independent of CS modality.
evidence: This is concluded from the absence of learning with both visual and whisker CS in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: GluA4 appears to be dispensable for the control of coordinated locomotion.
source: Thus, GluA4 appears to be dispensable for the control of coordinated locomotion (Figure 7), but is required for normal cerebellum-dependent associative learning.
evidence: This is concluded from the normal locomotion but impaired eyeblink conditioning in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: GluA4 is required for normal cerebellum-dependent associative learning.
source: Thus, GluA4 appears to be dispensable for the control of coordinated locomotion (Figure 7), but is required for normal cerebellum-dependent associative learning.
evidence: This is concluded from the impaired eyeblink conditioning in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: Deletion of GluA4 resulted in selective impairment of MF→GC transmission.
source: Deletion of GluA4 resulted in selective impairment of MF→GC transmission.
evidence: This is concluded from the strong reduction in MF→GC EPSCs but normal transmission at other cerebellar synapses.

claim: The pronounced decrease of AMPAR-mediated excitation caused a severe deficit in synaptic integration during high-frequency transmission in GluA4-KO GCs.
source: Despite compensatory changes in tonic inhibition and NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-mediated synaptic input, the pronounced decrease of AMPAR-mediated excitation caused a severe deficit in synaptic integration during high-frequency transmission.
evidence: This is concluded from the reduced spike output during high-frequency stimulation in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: The synaptic changes in GluA4-KO GCs impaired pattern separation and learning performance of a feedforward network model.
source: These synaptic changes impaired pattern separation and learning performance of a feedforward network model.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results showing reduced expansion coding and learning speed.

claim: GluA4-KO mice displayed normal locomotor coordination.
source: On a behavioral level, GluA4-KO mice displayed normal locomotor coordination, but a complete absence of eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: The manuscript presents locomotor analysis data in Figure 7 showing normal locomotion.

claim: GluA4-KO mice showed a complete absence of eyeblink conditioning.
source: On a behavioral level, GluA4-KO mice displayed normal locomotor coordination, but a complete absence of eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral data in Figure 8 showing no learning in eyeblink conditioning.

claim: The findings demonstrate the importance of the GluA4 AMPAR subunit for cerebellar input layer synaptic function and associative memory formation.
source: Our findings demonstrate the importance of the GluA4 AMPAR subunit for cerebellar input layer synaptic function and associative memory formation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental and modeling results presented.

claim: GluA4 shows a regional expression pattern in the CNS with the strongest detection in the cerebellum.
source: GluA4 shows a regional expression pattern in the CNS with the strongest detection in the cerebellum (Sjöstedt et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Sjöstedt et al., 2020).

claim: GluA4 has been described in Bergmann glia within the cerebellar cortex.
source: Within the cerebellar cortex, this AMPAR subunit has been described in Bergmann glia (Saab et al., 2012) and in GCs (Mosbacher et al., 1994), where GluA4 is the major AMPAR subunit at MF→GC synapses (Delvendahl et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Saab et al., 2012).

claim: Other AMPAR subunits cannot compensate for the loss of GluA4 in GluA4-KO mice.
source: The strongly diminished MF→GC EPSCs in GluA4-KO mice indicate that other AMPAR subunits cannot compensate for the loss of GluA4 (Yan et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the strong reduction in MF→GC EPSCs and supported by citations (Yan et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2011).

claim: The reduced inhibition in GluA4-KO mice may enhance sensory information transfer at the cerebellar input layer.
source: Our slice data of GC tonic inhibitory conductance are similar to observations in vivo (Duguid et al., 2012), where tonic inhibition controls GC excitability (Chadderton et al., 2004) and EPSC-spike coupling (Duguid et al., 2012). The reduced inhibition in GluA4-KO mice may thus enhance sensory information transfer at the cerebellar input layer.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced tonic inhibition and its known role in controlling GC excitability.

claim: Reduced α6 GABAAR expression contributes to the modulation of GC tonic inhibition upon loss of AMPARs.
source: These findings suggest that reduced α6 GABAAR expression contributes to the modulation of GC tonic inhibition upon loss of AMPARs.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced α6 GABAAR levels in GluA4-KO cerebella and previous findings in stargazer and waggler mice.

claim: The larger NMDAR-EPSCs in GluA4-KO are most likely caused by enhanced glutamate release driven by an increase in the number of presynaptic release sites.
source: The larger NMDAR-EPSCs in GluA4-KO are most likely caused by enhanced glutamate release (Chourbaji et al., 2008; Delvendahl et al., 2019) that is driven by an increase in the number of presynaptic release sites, but we cannot exclude postsynaptic contributions.
evidence: This is inferred from the SMAQ analysis showing increased release sites and supported by citations (Chourbaji et al., 2008; Delvendahl et al., 2019).

claim: Attenuated inhibition and enhanced NMDAR-EPSCs contribute to synaptic information transfer by increasing the excitability of GluA4-KO GCs.
source: Together, attenuated inhibition and enhanced NMDAR-EPSCs contribute to synaptic information transfer by increasing the excitability of GluA4-KO GCs.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of reduced inhibition, enhanced NMDAR transmission, and increased excitability.

claim: The adaptations in GluA4-KO GCs are insufficient for maintaining the fidelity of GC output at WT level.
source: Yet, these adaptations are insufficient for maintaining the fidelity of GC output at WT level.
evidence: This is concluded from the persistent deficits in spike output despite compensatory mechanisms.

claim: Attenuated tonic inhibition and enhanced non-AMPAR transmission may sustain sufficient levels of MF→GC transmission in GluA4-KO animals to spare locomotor activity.
source: This may point toward other pathways contributing to sensorimotor coordination or could be due to developmental compensation. It is intriguing to speculate that attenuated tonic inhibition and enhanced non-AMPAR transmission sustain sufficient levels of MF→GC transmission in GluA4-KO animals to spare locomotor activity.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed compensatory mechanisms and normal locomotion.

claim: The raised GC threshold might be overcome by activation of multiple MF inputs, which can increase GC spike rates in vivo.
source: The raised GC threshold might also be overcome by activation of multiple MF inputs, which can increase GC spike rates in vivo (Ishikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to previous work (Ishikawa et al., 2015).

claim: MF activity during locomotion is generally dense and may activate a sufficient number of GCs for locomotor coordination in GluA4-KO mice.
source: MF activity during locomotion is generally dense (Ishikawa et al., 2015; Knogler et al., 2017; Powell et al., 2015) and may thus activate a sufficient number of GCs for locomotor coordination in GluA4-KO mice.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous work (Ishikawa et al., 2015; Knogler et al., 2017; Powell et al., 2015).

claim: The MF representation of the CS used for eyeblink conditioning is most likely not widespread and dense enough to activate a critical fraction of GCs in GluA4-KO mice.
source: By contrast, the MF representation of the CS used for eyeblink conditioning is most likely not widespread and dense enough to activate a critical fraction of GCs in GluA4-KO mice (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Shimuta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous work (Giovannucci et al., 2017; Shimuta et al., 2020).

claim: A small number of active GCs may be sufficient for basic motor performance.
source: Indeed, a small number of active GCs may be sufficient for basic motor performance (Galliano et al., 2013; Schweighofer et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Galliano et al., 2013; Schweighofer et al., 2001).

claim: Disturbed AMPAR trafficking at MF→GC synapses in ataxic stargazer mice compromises eyeblink conditioning.
source: Indeed, disturbed AMPAR trafficking at MF→GC, as well as other cerebellar synapses, in ataxic stargazer mice compromises eyeblink conditioning (Hashimoto et al., 1999; Jackson and Nicoll, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Hashimoto et al., 1999; Jackson and Nicoll, 2011).

claim: The findings in GluA4-KO mice support a role of MF→GC synapses in cerebellar associative learning.
source: Our findings in GluA4-KO mice further support a role of MF→GC synapses in cerebellar associative learning.
evidence: This is concluded from the impaired eyeblink conditioning in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: The expression of GluA4 is generally low in the mammalian CNS outside of the cerebellum.
source: However, the expression of GluA4 is generally low in the mammalian CNS outside of the cerebellum (Hadzic et al., 2017; Schwenk et al., 2014; Sjöstedt et al., 2020; Yamasaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Hadzic et al., 2017; Schwenk et al., 2014; Sjöstedt et al., 2020; Yamasaki et al., 2011).

claim: GluA4 is expressed in Bergmann glia, but deletion of AMPARs in these cells does not affect eyeblink conditioning.
source: Besides, GluA4 is expressed in Bergmann glia, but deletion of AMPARs in these cells does not affect eyeblink conditioning (Saab et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Saab et al., 2012).

claim: Associative memory formation during eyeblink conditioning takes place within the cerebellum.
source: Although we cannot rule out a contribution from other GluA4-containing synapses elsewhere in the brain, associative memory formation during eyeblink conditioning takes place within the cerebellum (Carey, 2011; De Zeeuw and Yeo, 2005; Freeman and Steinmetz, 2011; Heiney et al., 2014; Mauk, 1997; McCormick and Thompson, 1984), where GluA4 is predominantly expressed in GCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Carey, 2011; De Zeeuw and Yeo, 2005; Freeman and Steinmetz, 2011; Heiney et al., 2014; Mauk, 1997; McCormick and Thompson, 1984).

claim: The properties of the GluA4 AMPAR subunit are likely to be important for transmission and processing of the CS at the MF→GC synapse.
source: At this synaptic connection, the properties of the GluA4 AMPAR subunit are likely to be important for transmission and processing of the CS, which is conveyed by MF inputs (Albergaria et al., 2018; De Zeeuw and Yeo, 2005; Mauk, 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the role of MF inputs in conveying the CS and the importance of GluA4 for MF→GC transmission, supported by citations (Albergaria et al., 2018; De Zeeuw and Yeo, 2005; Mauk, 1997).

claim: Locomotor coordination can be sustained by low levels of GC-population activity and may rely on effective population sparsening.
source: These findings indicate that locomotor coordination can be sustained by low levels of GC-population activity, and may rely on effective population sparsening.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal locomotion despite reduced GC activity and maintained sparseness in GluA4-KO mice.

claim: Associative memory formation may require more complex levels of GC activity and/or synaptic integration than locomotor coordination.
source: In contrast, associative memory formation may require more complex levels of GC activity and/or synaptic integration (Albergaria et al., 2018; Carey, 2011; Raymond and Medina, 2018).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous work (Albergaria et al., 2018; Carey, 2011; Raymond and Medina, 2018).

claim: The longer spike delay in GluA4-KO mice, together with the reduced MF→GC synaptic strength, raises the threshold of GC activation, which leads to a loss of information.
source: The longer spike delay in GluA4-KO mice, together with the reduced MF→GC synaptic strength, raises the threshold of GC activation, which leads to a loss of information (Billings et al., 2014; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased spike delay and reduced synaptic strength, supported by citations (Billings et al., 2014; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017).

claim: GC spikes upon onset of the CS might arrive too late to trigger a CR due to the longer delay in GluA4-KO mice.
source: Due to a longer delay, GC spikes upon onset of the CS might also arrive too late to trigger a CR.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the increased spike delay in GluA4-KO GCs.

claim: The alterations of MF→GC transmission in the absence of GluA4 could reduce the reliability and increase the temporal variability of PF-driven PC excitation in response to sensory stimulation.
source: Furthermore, the alterations of MF→GC transmission in the absence of GluA4 could reduce the reliability and increase the temporal variability of PF-driven PC excitation in response to sensory stimulation, which may interfere with synaptic plasticity at PF→PC synapses (Suvrathan and Raymond, 2018).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to previous work (Suvrathan and Raymond, 2018).

claim: The higher GC threshold in GluA4-KO mice impaired expansion recoding of MF inputs onto the large population of GCs by effectively reducing the coding space.
source: Our modeling results suggest that the higher GC threshold impaired expansion recoding of MF inputs onto the large population of GCs (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969) by effectively reducing the coding space.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results showing reduced total variance, supported by citations (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969).

claim: The effective rise of the GC threshold due to weak MF input strength may decrease overlap between GC outputs, which would be predicted to improve learning speed.
source: On the other hand, the effective rise of the GC threshold due to weak MF input strength may by itself decrease overlap between GC outputs, which would be predicted to improve learning speed (Marr, 1969).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to theoretical work (Marr, 1969).

claim: The findings are consistent with the hypothesis that pattern separation at the cerebellar input layer promotes associative memory formation.
source: Together, our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that pattern separation at the cerebellar input layer promotes associative memory formation.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental and modeling results showing impaired expansion coding and learning.

claim: The results provide further evidence for the concept of an AMPAR code, in which different AMPAR subunits serve different roles for synaptic function and learning.
source: The results we present here provide further evidence for the concept of an AMPAR code (Diering and Huganir, 2018), in which different AMPAR subunits serve different roles for synaptic function and learning.
evidence: This is concluded from the specific role of GluA4 in cerebellar function and learning, supported by citation (Diering and Huganir, 2018).
